content:
I'd like to share with this community my recently completed bachelors thesis in which I formalize the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal construction in Lean. Although this code has already been in Mathlib for some time, I just graduated with my bachelors degree and so I have this completed document which I can share:

Formalizing_the_Gelfand_Naimark_Segal_Construction_in_Lean_final.pdf

I am mainly sharing this to express my gratitude for this community, particularly @Jireh Loreaux and @Monica Omar, but also because I do have an opportunity to make some edits before the document is uploaded permanently to my institution's senior thesis repository. So, if anyone feels inclined to look through this document and spots any serious errors (i.e. anything false as stated or improperly attributed), please let me know so I can fix it as soon as possible. (Of course, this document has already been read and reviewed by multiple people, so I'd hope/expect that there are no such errors, and I've done my best to ensure that there are no such errors.)

This Zulip community was an invaluable resource while learning Lean and working on this project, so thank you to everyone who has ever responded to any of my questions here or had public conversations on Zulip with information that helped me better understand Lean, formalization, or Mathlib.

Congratulations on your senior thesis! Just to try and understand the background of this: did you have no lean expert supervising you locally at your institution, and have had to just rely on feedback from mathlib reviewers in order to get the code over the line and to learn various tricks involved in formalisation?

Yes, as soon as I started learning lean, I essentially became my institution's leading lean expert, and feedback from Mathlib reviewers is how I learned most of what I learned about formalization, Lean, and Mathlib. My advisor was a CS professor with experience in software verification, programming languages, and type theory, but minimal direct experience with lean.

Gregory Wickham said:

Yes, as soon as I started learning lean, I essentially became my institution's leading lean expert, and feedback from Mathlib reviewers is how I learned most of what I learned about formalization, Lean, and Mathlib. My advisor was a CS professor with experience in software verification, programming languages, and type theory, but minimal direct experience with lean.

Out of interest as someone coming from a non-Lean institution , did you happen to end up inspiring anyone at your institution to also take up Lean?

I'm not sure how much responsibility I can claim for inspiring anyone, but I know that there is at least one student still at my institution, who seemed interested in lean and to whom I've spoken about the process of getting code into Mathlib, so I can hope that I've inspired them to continue using and learning more about lean.

Congratulations on the thesis Gregory. I am surprised to hear that there are no lean experts at Harvey Mudd, and I am glad that you are getting the word out!

Gregory Wickham said:

if anyone feels inclined to look through this document and spots any serious errors (i.e. anything false as stated or improperly attributed), please let me know so I can fix it as soon as possible.

I do spot one mistake, I think. On pg. 30, you write:

[IsUniformAddGroup α] and [IsUniformAddGroup β] ensure that addition and negation on α and β are uniformly continuous with respect to their structure as a UniformSpace. This is equivalent to
stating that α and β are topological additive groups.

I am concerned about that last sentence. Mathlib has a seperate definition docs#IsTopologicalAddGroup and in general this is not equivalent to [IsUniformAddGroup α]. As explained in the docstring for docs#IsUniformAddGroup, these two are equivalent only when the given uniformity (from [UniformSpace α]) coincides with the induced right/left uniformity from docs#IsTopologicalAddGroup.leftUniformSpace.

Thank you. You're right. I shouldn't have said equivalent. What I meant was that saying α is a uniform additive group implies that it is a topological additive group. So, it's a stronger, not equivalent condition. I'll change that last sentence to say "This ensures that α and β are topological additive groups."
A small typo in Definition 3.1.1 on page 27: instead of f(cx)=σ(x)f(x)f(cx) = \sigma(x) f(x)f(cx)=σ(x)f(x), it should make more sense as f(cx)=σ(c)f(x)f(cx) = \sigma(c)f(x)f(cx)=σ(c)f(x)
Thank you! I really should have caught that one.

Jack McCarthy said:

[IsUniformAddGroup α] and [IsUniformAddGroup β] ensure that addition and negation on α and β are uniformly continuous with respect to their structure as a UniformSpace. This is equivalent to
stating that α and β are topological additive groups.

I am concerned about that last sentence. Mathlib has a seperate definition docs#IsTopologicalAddGroup and in general this is not equivalent to [IsUniformAddGroup α]. As explained in the docstring for docs#IsUniformAddGroup, these two are equivalent only when the given uniformity (from [UniformSpace α]) coincides with the induced right/left uniformity from docs#IsTopologicalAddGroup.leftUniformSpace.

They agree for commutative groups though, which is often implicitly implied by "additive group".

My understanding was that even with commutativity you still need agreement between the two uniform structures [UniformSpace α] == IsTopologicalGroup.rightUniformSpace (since the latter is used in the definition of docs#isUniformGroup_of_commGroup).

As a counter-example, you could take a copy of ℝ and induce uniformity by a metric d(x,y)=∣arctan⁡(x)−arctan⁡(y)∣d(x,y) = |\arctan(x) - \arctan(y)|d(x,y)=∣arctan(x)−arctan(y)∣. Then this space IsTopologicalAddGroup, UniformSpace, AddCommGroup, but not IsUniformAddGroup since subtraction is not uniformly continuous. E.g. notice that d(n,n+1)→0d(n, n+1) \to 0d(n,n+1)→0 and d(n,n)=0d(n, n) = 0d(n,n)=0, yet d(n−n,n+1−n)=d(0,1)=π/4d(n-n, n+1-n) = d(0,1) = \pi/4d(n−n,n+1−n)=d(0,1)=π/4.
you need IsTopologicalAddGroup, and you need the uniformity to coincide with both IsTopologicalAddGroup.leftUniformSpace and IsTopologicalAddGroup.rightUniformSpace
Exactly. The latter two always coincide (since we assume commutativity) but that doesn't mean they coincide with our original uniformity.
